newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-DE LA HOYA OUTPOINTS WHITAKER FOR WBC WELTERWEIGHT CROWN.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-DE LA HOYA OUTPOINTS WHITAKER FOR WBC WELTERWEIGHT CROWN.

text.p: Oscar de la Hoya kept his record perfect and claimed a world title in a fourth different weight class by capturing Pernell Whitaker's World Boxing Council welterweight crown with a unanimous decision on Saturday night.

It was the first fight in the welterweight division for de la Hoya, who also holds the WBC super welterweight title and has previously won the International Boxing Federation's junior lightweight, lightweight belts.
"I thought it was a close fight but I believe I did more than enough to win," said de la Hoya, who raised his record to 24-0 and furthered his claim as the world's best boxer, pound-for-pound.
Judges Jerry Roth and Dalby Shirley scored the fight 116-110, while Chuck Giampa had it 115-111 for de la Hoya.
Whitaker, who was making his ninth defence of the WBC welterweight crown, fell to 40-2-1 with his first defeat in more than nine years.
"I told you all along that his southpaw style was going to give me problems and it did. He's by far the hardest I've ever faced," the popular de la Hoya admitted.
De la Hoya suffered the fight's only knockdown in the ninth round when Whitaker caught him with a left hook on the side of the neck, putting the challenger on one knee.
"He didn't hurt me in the fight and he certainly didn't hurt me with that knockdown," de la Hoya claimed.
The 33-year-old Whitaker had not lost a fight since dropping a controversial decision to Jose Ramirez in Paris in March, 1988 -- a defeat he avenged with ease 18 months later.
"Oscar is a good fighter but there's no way I lost this fight," said a bitter Whitaker.
"I thought it was a blowout, a shutout, I couldn't have been better. I should have gotten 10 of the 12 rounds," Whitaker complained.
"It was the old Pernell Whitaker, the movement, the pizzazz, the ring generalship. The people saw it, I saw it, the world saw it. I want a rematch," he demanded.
Many ringside observers agreed with Whitaker's assessment of the fight, especially given his superior movement in the ring and ability to make de la Hoya miss.
The statistics showed Whitaker landing 232 of 258 of his punches, with de la Hoya connecting on 191 of 557.

At times Whitaker made de la Hoya look like a frustrated batter unable to get his bat on a pitcher's fast ball. Often he had de la Hoya throwing punches and places Whitaker had been seconds before, but had since vacated.
De la Hoya did appear to score with many more power punches than Whitaker, however, and likely won a lot of rounds with flurries of combination in the final 30 seconds.
"I felt that once I did land some shots that they hurt him and I thought that they gave me enough to take those rounds," de la Hoya said.
"Even though he made me miss at times, I thought most of the rounds I finished with good combinations, especially in the last two rounds."
De la Hoya, the beneficiary of an accidental head-butt in the third round that cost Whitaker a point, seemed more than willing to satisfy the former champion's demands.
"I'll give him the rematch anytime, anywhere," de la Hoya said. "I'm frustrated because I can do better, much better."
